3	
4	Vision token pruning is one of the most reliable efficiency techniques in Vision Transformer (ViT) inference: DynamicViT~\cite{rao2021dynamicvit} removes 66\% of tokens with $<$0.5\% accuracy loss, ToMe~\cite{bolya2023tome} merges 40\% at $>$99\% accuracy, and EViT~\cite{liang2022evit} discards 50\% with negligible degradation. These results have established a strong prior that vision tokens are highly redundant. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~\cite{brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,ghosh2024octo,shukor2025smolvla} use the same ViT encoders, producing hundreds of tokens that dominate the LLM backbone's input. For real-time robotic control at 5--10 Hz, reducing these tokens would yield immediate speedups in the quadratically scaling attention computation. Several recent works explore this direction: FastV~\cite{chen2024fastv} prunes inattentive VLM tokens, VLA-Cache~\cite{xu2025vlacache} caches vision tokens across timesteps, and VLA-IAP~\cite{cheng2026vlaiap} proposes importance-aware VLA pruning.
5	
6	However, no prior work has systematically evaluated how vision token reduction behaves across different VLA architectures in closed-loop control, where a single corrupted action can push the robot off-trajectory and subsequent errors compound irrecoverably. Existing evaluations rely on offline metrics (action loss, perplexity) that average over independent timesteps and fail to capture this compounding failure mode.

tool_args.old_string:
\paragraph{Vision connectors.}
Per-patch MLP projectors~\cite{liu2023llava,kim2024openvla} preserve per-token granularity. Cross-attention connectors (Q-Former~\cite{li2023blip2}, Perceiver~\cite{alayrac2022flamingo,jaegle2021perceiver}) compress to learned queries at the architectural level. Pixel-shuffle connectors~\cite{shi2016subpixel,shukor2025smolvla,chen2024internvl} fold patches via channel concatenation, achieving training-time compression but creating inter-token dependencies. Our analysis links this taxonomy to inference-time compressibility and shows that cross-attention re-encoding can overcome the failure mode of deletion on pixel-shuffle architectures.

tool_args.old_string: Offline evaluation metrics (importance margins, per-step action loss) provide misleadingly positive signals during pruning. The gap arises because offline metrics average over independent timesteps, while closed-loop execution compounds errors: a single corrupted action pushes the robot off-trajectory, subsequent observations diverge from training data, and recovery becomes impossible. In our single-step analysis, pruning produces 111.5\% relative action error with complete gripper inversion (Table~\ref{tab:offline_action_error}, Appendix~\ref{app:offline_error}). These failures are rare enough to be averaged away in offline metrics but fatal in any episode where they occur. Closed-loop evaluation is a necessary validation step for any VLA compression method.
tool_args.new_string: Offline evaluation metrics average over independent timesteps and fail to capture the binary nature of closed-loop failure. While the aggregate $3.4\times$ action error increase (Table~\ref{tab:offline_action_error}, Appendix~\ref{app:offline_error}) is clearly a negative signal, standard per-step metrics do not distinguish between moderate perturbations (position errors of 0.20--0.30 per axis) and catastrophic events (complete gripper inversion, L2 = 1.02) that are individually sufficient to terminate an episode. In closed-loop execution, a single catastrophic action pushes the robot off-trajectory, subsequent observations diverge from training data, and recovery becomes impossible. These catastrophic events are rare enough to be diluted in per-step averages but occur in every pruned episode we tested. Closed-loop evaluation is a necessary validation step for any VLA compression method.

Both Smart Compress and the baseline start from the same pretrained checkpoint (SmolVLA-Base) and train for 100K steps with identical hyperparameters; the only architectural difference is the 22.2M-parameter cross-attention compressor (Smart Compress trains 122.1M total parameters including the expert action head, vs.\ 99.9M for the baseline).

To further isolate the re-encoding effect, we trained a matched control: the same base checkpoint with 100K additional training steps and identical hyperparameters but without the compressor module. This extended baseline achieves 45.0\% SR (Table~\ref{tab:smart_compress}), statistically indistinguishable from the original 44.8\% baseline ($p > 0.9$, two-proportion $z$-test), confirming that the performance gain originates from the cross-attention architecture rather than additional training compute.\footnote{The extended baseline also collapses to 0\% SR under pruning ($k{=}0.50$, random, true removal), confirming that additional training does not mitigate the pixel-shuffle vulnerability.}

Table~\ref{tab:smart_compress} reports all five Smart Compress configurations. The cross-attention module improves performance regardless of compression: $M \in \{32, 64, 128\}$ all achieve $\sim$60\% SR, exceeding the 44.8\% baseline by 15--17 points ($p < 0.001$, two-proportion $z$-test). The $M = 128$ passthrough (59.8\% SR, no compression) matches $M = 32$ (61.6\%, 75\% reduction), establishing that the gain originates from re-encoding, not compression. Only at $M = 16$ (87.5\% compression) does performance decline modestly to 55.8\%, still 11 points above baseline. Across two random seeds, $M{=}32$ achieves 60.4\% $\pm$ 1.2, $M{=}64$ achieves 60.8\% $\pm$ 0.8, and $M{=}96$ achieves 55.4\% $\pm$ 2.8, confirming robustness to initialization. The $M{=}96$ dip may reflect an intermediate bottleneck that introduces representational redundancy without the regularization benefit of stronger compression ($M{=}32$, $M{=}64$). In the same setting where every hard pruning method produces 0\%, the worst Smart Compress configuration exceeds the uncompressed baseline (Figure~\ref{fig:results_combined}b). To evaluate generalization, we test the $M{=}32$ model (trained on LIBERO-Object) on two unseen suites: LIBERO-Spatial (53.2\% SR) and LIBERO-Goal (56.4\% SR), compared to 0\% under hard pruning on both suites (Table~\ref{tab:cross_suite}, Appendix). While LIBERO-Goal shows a 6.6 percentage point decrease relative to the unpruned baseline (63.0\%), Smart Compress maintains non-trivial performance where deletion-based methods completely fail.
